Toward the end of this process, you apply for admission into the nursing major itself. At that point, all they are looking at is your prior year (for an ADN/ASN) or two years (for a BSN) of coursework and related activities. As a result, pre-nursing programs tend to not be very competitive to enter. For some, admission to the college or university is sufficient. For ASN/ADM programs, anybody who can enroll at the community college can begin the pre-nursing program. Generally, my point is this: you're thinking in terms of honors and AP being accolades that will be valuable, but that hasn't been my experience. many colleges and universities require that students take the three core natural sciences: biology, chemistry, and physics. If you have not taken physics but you have taken regular chemistry, you should probably take physics, regardless of whether it's AP, honors, or regular. I suspect that to maximize your chances of admission, your schedule should look something like this: pre-calculus, senior English, physics, history, and foreign language. Question: How do I tell my parents I’m struggling in school and want to switch schools?
Old_Answer: If you trust your parents, and you probably should, I would recommend starting with the first part: "mom, dad, I'm struggling in school." Maybe write down a few points to help you remember how to describe your struggle. Is it grades? Social Issues? Not feeling like you're learning? Feel like you could do better elsewhere? Once you describe what the issues are to your parents, explain that you feel there's a need for change you can have your suggested outcome, presumably transferring to a different school (perhaps one identified), but your parents may have better advice. Often parents offer this "advice": work harder. It's not ill intention, but it's also not actionable. At that point you can ask, "can you help me with that?" Now if you really feel that the solution is to a particular different school, you should outline why that school is a better choice for you in the short and long terms. Again, write this down before you talk to your parents; just winging it is not a great way for a child convince adults. Don't forget to consider the long-term consequences; an academically less rigorous school might leave you less prepared for the next stage of your academic or professional life. What will you do then?

Question: How beneficial is it to pursue education until a PhD for an industrial career?
Old_Answer: In a small number of fields, pursuing a PhD can open some doors that would otherwise be closed without also closing some doors. For example, someone with a PhD in computer science (if their research skills were exceptional and aligned with the work of the company) get a research job at a private company. Until recently, someone with a CS PhD and the right problem-solving skills could also get a software engineering job, often starting at a higher level than new hires without post graduate degrees. Beyond that, a PhD is rarely the best way to maximize your earnings. Yes, there are some people in industry research in many fields, some of whom are very well paid, but with few exceptions, someone who earned a PhD could have chosen a more financially rewarding career path that required less education.

In some industries, particularly in research and development sectors, having a PhD can open doors to advanced positions that require deep expertise and innovative thinking. Employers often seek candidates with a PhD for roles that involve complex problem-solving and cutting-edge research, as these individuals are typically seen as thought leaders. However, it's important to recognize that not all industries place the same value on a PhD. In many cases, practical experience and skills can outweigh academic credentials. For instance, in tech or engineering fields, hands-on experience, internships, and a strong portfolio can be more advantageous than a PhD. Additionally, the time and financial investment required for a PhD should not be underestimated. It can take several years to complete, during which you might miss out on valuable industry experience and networking opportunities. Ultimately, if your goal is to engage in high-level research or to teach at a university, a PhD is essential. But if you aim to work in a more applied setting, consider whether a master's degree or even just relevant work experience might better serve your career aspirations. Assess your personal goals, the demands of your desired industry, and weigh the pros and cons carefully before committing to a PhD program.

Question: How might a HS Sophmore start a volunteer abroad program? I'd really like to give my classmates the chance to help out others in less developed countries. What might the costs and supplies look like? Any ideas of fundraisers to help out with money?
Old_Answer: Money and connections. That's why these "volunteer abroad" programs only briefly had any impact on admission to the self-styled "elite" colleges and universities; they quickly realized that these were more functions of parents spending money than students really caring about digging Wells in South America or Africa. There are plenty of programs that will give you a volunteering abroad experience in exchange for a few thousand dollars. Whether the costs are legitimate or not, I don't know, but you will definitely travel to some other country and dig Wells or do something similar. Many churches have mission programs, some of which will involve students, but given the complexities of volunteering abroad and the tendency of young people to be… well, young people, you typically have to be involved for a long time. You don't necessarily have to be religious, I suppose, just involved in a mission group's work. What kind of costs would this require? Assuming you are connecting with an existing program, you can just act as a front. The costs are on the order of a few thousand dollars per student. If you genuinely want to build something new, I suspect it would require hundreds of thousands of dollars, plus connections. If your parents are involved in national government or international business, they can probably get you started. My suggestion is this. Pick something that you care about, and something related to your local community (construed broadly, so it could be your metro area). Then start volunteering. Once you start volunteering, recruit your friends to join you. Figure out how you as a group of young young people can have impact on your local community. raising a few thousand dollars great, but it's rarely a profound importance. The most profound accomplishment would be to create an ongoing, self-sustaining volunteering organization or pipeline for high school students. Unfortunately, many high schools have instituted "service learning" requirements, which sound nice on paper but end up being a little value.
